sweep_summary: zigu1244 Zigula-Mushungulu is not in the catalog. All four stress/accent title hits are closed: Kisseberth 1992 (Via Afrika Festschrift, print-only; Google Books snippet only) and Kenstowicz 1989 (Certamen phonologicum, print-only; not on Kenstowicz's MIT page) are the two high-priority acquisitions — both are the primary Tanzanian Chizigula accent/tone analyses; Philippson 1991/92 thesis (theses.fr: accessible = non; abstract read: ~30 East African Bantu languages, penult demarcative accent as evolutionary driver) is medium priority, and its derivative Philippson 1998 (Persée, altcha-gated) is Downing 2004's source for 'Chizigula: penult stress, tonal'; Bamba 1992 (UQAM, 672 pp, not in Archipel) is per a 1992 'Linguistique africaine' snippet a Mande-domain tone-accent thesis with Kizigua and Guéré as extra cases — low priority. Readable first-hand evidence (all already held by the project from the earlier reading, re-read and page-pinned here): Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990:166/171 via Hyman 2009:195 — penult is an abstract accent that attracts H from the left, no stress cues except phrase-final length; Hout 2012:6/49 — penultimate lengthening 'caused by stress assignment' to the utterance penult; Hout 2020:39 — consistent utterance-penult lengthening usually with a high pitch target, tone marginal in Somali Mushunguli; Meinhof 1906:289 (page image verified) — 'mechanical' stress on the antepenult 'at least in many cases', tone present. Downing 2004:120 codes Chizigula as penult stress-accent + tone. StressTyp2 has no Zigula entry. Recommended coding if added: tonal, penultimate (phrase-final) prominence via tone attraction and lengthening, no lexical word stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence is penultimate: the penult of a word said in isolation / of an utterance is lengthened (extra mora) and usually carries a high pitch target; the utterance-final syllable cannot be long. Hout's earlier thesis (2012: 6, 48) words the same fact as 'Penultimate Lengthening occurs when stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable of an utterance'. For Tanzanian Zigula, Kenstowicz & Kisseberth (1990: 166, quoted verbatim in Hyman 2009: 195) treat the penult as the accented syllable in an abstract sense: it attracts H tone from its left but 'does not have increased duration (except in phrase-final position), nor is it necessarily raised in pitch'. Downing (2004, table 15) codes Chizigula as penult stress-accent, tonal, citing Philippson 1998. Discordant older note: Meinhof (1906: 289) heard the 'mechanische Ton' on the antepenult 'wenigstens in vielen Faellen' (probably the antepenultimate H of some verb tenses, cf. Pillion 2013: a word's H falls on the penult or antepenult).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described in any source examined. (Downing 2004: 129 and K&K 1990 note some H tones shift to the stem-initial syllable in Chizigula, a tonal, not stress, effect.)
new_statements.exceptions: Hout 2020: nouns elicited in isolation only variably show penult lengthening (list intonation); utterance-final syllables are never long (compensatory lengthening blocked there); words inside a phrase lose the lengthening (Hout 2012: 7, mwaana vs mwana ywaangu, with free variation). Meinhof 1906 reports antepenult stress 'in many cases' for Tanzanian Zigula.
new_statements.domain_note: The durational cue is utterance/phrase-level: penult of the utterance (= the word in citation form). Word-internally in Tanzanian Zigula the penult's prominence is tonal (target of H shift) per Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990; Mushunguli (Somali dialect) has largely lost tone (Hout 2020: 50). Citation forms therefore show penult length (+ high pitch); phrase-medial words need not.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 zigu1244 'Zigula-Mushungulu' (ISO ziw) has two dialects: zigu1242 Zigula (Tanzania) and mush1238 Mushungulu = Mushunguli / Somali Chizigula (ISO xma, lower Jubba, Somalia; diaspora in US). The quoted statement (Hout 2020) and Hout 2012 / Pillion 2013 describe the Somali dialect Mushunguli (mush1238), from one primary consultant born in Mogambo; Hout reports tone there is 'at best moribund'. Meinhof 1906 and the tonological literature (Kenstowicz 1989; Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990; Kisseberth 1992) describe Tanzanian Zigula (zigu1242), which is fully tonal with H attracted to the penult. Glottolog lists Hout 2012 and Pillion 2013 as University of Kansas theses; both are Ohio State University B.A. theses (OSU Knowledge Bank).

new_statements.reading: Zigula/Chizigula has penultimate prominence, but of an abstract kind: the penult attracts H tone (long-distance shift, K&K 1990:171) and is lengthened only at utterance/phrase end (Hout 2020:39; Hout 2012:6 calls this 'stress assigned to the penultimate syllable of an utterance'); there is no word-level durational or pitch stress cue. For catalog purposes: tonal language with penultimate (phrase-final) prominence / penult-accent tone attraction, not lexical stress. Meinhof 1906:289 (antepenult 'in many cases') is an early impressionistic outlier. None of the four title-hit items (Kisseberth 1992, Kenstowicz 1989, Philippson 1991, Bamba 1992) is open; Kisseberth 1992 and Kenstowicz 1989 remain the highest-priority acquisitions.

readall_conflicts: The only conflict on record is the one already noted in the on-disk check: Meinhof 1906 (MSOS 9, sec. 8 Betonung, p. 289) gives antepenultimate stress 'in many cases' for Tanzanian Zigula, against the penultimate prominence reported by Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990 (via Hyman 2009:195), Downing 2004 table (15) citing Philippson 1998, and Hout 2020:39 for Mushunguli; our earlier reading treats Meinhof as an early impressionistic outlier. The Philippson 1992 abstract is compatible with the penultimate reading but says nothing about Zigula itself.

sources.quote: The lengthening of the penultimate syllable here is due to the fact that this phrase was elicited in isolation: the penultimate syllable of any utterance is also lengthened, as illustrated by the examples in (6). This is usually, but not always, associated with a high pitch target; while penultimate lengthening is quite consistent, tone and intonation are not. (6) Penultimate lengthening a. sidumuːla 'I chopped' b. sikemoː m̩piːra 'I threw the ball' c. sikemeː mipira kʷaːmajoːɳɖa 'I threw the balls to the baboons'. sources.locator: ch. 2, sec. 2.2.2 'Vowels', p. 39, with examples (6) 'Penultimate lengthening'
sources.note: Sec. 2.2.2 p.39: the penultimate syllable of any utterance is lengthened (examples sidumuːla 'I chopped', sikemoː m̩piːra 'I threw the ball'), 'usually, but not always, associated with a high pitch target'; nouns in isolation only variably lengthened; final syllable of an utterance may not be long. Sec. 2.2.5 p.50: Tanzanian Chizigula described as tonal (Kenstowicz 1989, K&K 1990, Kisseberth 1992) but in Mushunguli tone is 'at best moribund'; tone not transcribed. The word 'stress' is not used for Mushunguli.

sources.note: Second-hand but verbatim from the primary Tanzanian Chizigula source: the penultimate syllable is the prominent ('accented') position — H tone shifts long-distance to the penult — but this accent is abstract: no durational cue except phrase-finally and no obligatory pitch raising. Supports coding as penult prominence / tone-attraction rather than phonetic stress.

sources.quote: 8. In betreff der Betonung ist zu beachten, daß der mechanische Ton hier nicht wie im Suaheli auf der vorletzten, sondern auf der drittletzten liegt, wenigstens in vielen Fällen. Auch scheint es mir, daß die Vokale viel kürzer abgerissen werden als im Suaheli. Der musikalische Ton ist, so viel ich sehe, nachzuweisen. [EN: As regards stress, note that the dynamic accent here lies not, as in Swahili, on the penultimate but on the antepenultimate, at least in many cases. It also seems to me that the vowels are cut off much shorter than in Swahili. Musical tone can, as far as I can see, be demonstrated.]
sources.note: Earliest first-hand statement (Tanzanian Zigula, 1906): dynamic stress on the antepenult 'in many cases', contrasting with Swahili penult; tone present. Conflicts with the modern penult-prominence analyses (K&K 1990; Hout 2012/2020) — likely reflects H-tone attraction to the penult being heard as antepenult prominence, or phrase-medial vs isolation forms; treat as historical, superseded.
